title: FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving

Title:FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: this https URL.

report.summary: FlashOffloading moves the entire KV cache to host DRAM with overlapped compute-load kernels and sparse indexing, boosting long-context LLM serving throughput under a 30 ms TPOT budget.
report.background: Long-context inference makes the KV cache grow linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so serving systems quickly exhaust HBM capacity and are forced to cap batch sizes. The standard workaround is offloading KV cache blocks to host DRAM, but every decode step then needs host-to-device transfers plus index lookups, and that overhead often cancels out the concurrency gains. Meanwhile PD-disaggregated architectures separate prefill and decode onto different pools, MTP/speculative decoding adds further memory pressure, and operators increasingly deploy on non-NVIDIA accelerators such as Ascend. The result is that raw concurrency numbers look good on paper while effective throughput under a strict time-per-output-token SLO stagnates. FlashOffloading targets precisely this gap by redesigning cache management across the whole pipeline rather than optimizing a single stage.
key_points: The bottleneck is memory, not compute: KV cache grows with both sequence length and batch size, so long-context serving hits the HBM capacity wall and concurrency collapses before the GPU's math units are saturated.

Full offloading across both phases: unlike schemes that only offload during decode, FlashOffloading keeps the whole KV cache in host DRAM and builds a rolling HBM cache for prefill plus a hot cache for decode, so neither phase is left uncatered for.
Zero-overhead miss lookup: a reverse sparse index lets the system locate offloaded blocks without extra lookup cost on the critical path, removing one of the classic latency taxes of tiered caching.
Compute-load overlap: a custom kernel overlaps H2D transfers with ongoing computation, hiding transfer latency behind useful work instead of serializing them.
Measured gains: on GLM-5.2 with MTP3 speculative decoding over an Ascend910C PD-disaggregated platform, prefill throughput rises up to 1.38x and decode up to 1.91x while holding a 30 ms TPOT SLO.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reinforces that long-context serving is now a memory-hierarchy engineering problem rather than a pure model problem: cheap host DRAM becomes a first-class tier in the serving stack, which can lower cost per token without new silicon. For developers, the techniques matter most where HBM is scarce or expensive, such as multi-tenant inference platforms and domestic accelerators, and the open-source integration means the ideas can be tested rather than just read. For regular users, the practical effect is that very long prompts, large document Q&A and agentic workloads with heavy context reuse can stay interactive instead of degrading as concurrency rises, with latency held to a predictable budget.
report.tools: Watch LMCache and Mooncake for KV cache tiering and disaggregated serving, vLLM and SGLang (HiCache) for prefix caching and offload integrations, and TensorRT-LLM for NVIDIA-side equivalents. On Ascend hardware, check MindIE and the paper's linked open-source serving framework. For benchmarking, use vLLM's benchmark harness or Locust-style load generators with explicit TPOT SLOs so throughput numbers reflect real latency constraints.
